_note: Flight profiles for /launches/flight/. Event times (seconds after liftoff) are from the cited mission page where 'source' is set; otherwise the profile is generic (typical sequence, rounded times) and says so on the page. Altitude/speed keypoints [t s, altitude km, speed km/h] are always Full Duplex estimates for the animation, never telemetry.

profiles.title: Vulcan VC6L · Amazon Leo LV-01

source.label: ULA, Vulcan Leo 1 mission page (flight profile graphic)

profiles.payload_note: ULA’s mission page says this flight carries 40 Amazon Leo satellites, released over about 26 minutes into orbits about 420 to 465 km up, inclined 51.9°.
events: Two BE-4 engines plus six solid rocket boosters push Vulcan off the pad.
Vulcan passes the speed of sound.
Peak aerodynamic stress: the moment the air pushes hardest on the rocket.
Four of the six spent solid boosters fall away.
The last two solid boosters fall away.
The first stage’s BE-4 engines shut down. Vulcan’s booster isn’t recovered on this flight.
The Centaur V upper stage separates from the booster.
The nose cone splits open, exposing the satellites to space.
Centaur reaches a first parking orbit and coasts for about 49 minutes.
A short burn to shape the deployment orbit.
Centaur is in the orbit where the satellites will be released.
Centaur starts releasing Amazon Leo satellites one batch at a time.
All satellites released. From here each one uses its own thrusters to climb to its working orbit over the coming weeks.
Centaur fires again to move itself out of the way.

profiles.title: Falcon 9 · Starlink

source.label: SpaceX, Starlink 15-20 mission page (published timeline; ‘all times approximate’)

profiles.basis: Based on SpaceX’s published timeline for Starlink 15-20, the previous launch in the same Starlink group from the same pad. SpaceX publishes each mission’s own timeline shortly before launch.
profiles.payload_note: SpaceX says Starlink 15-20 carried 27 satellites. This mission’s count is confirmed on launch day.
events: Nine Merlin engines lift Falcon 9 off the pad.
Peak aerodynamic stress on the rocket.
The first stage’s nine engines shut down.
The second stage’s single engine lights.
The two fairing halves fall away; SpaceX recovers them from the sea.
The first stage relights three engines to slow down as it falls back through the atmosphere.
The first stage lands on a droneship at sea, ready to fly again.
The second stage reaches orbit and coasts.
A one-second burn to trim the orbit.
The whole stack of flat-packed Starlink satellites is released at once. They then drift apart and use their own thrusters to spread out and climb.

profiles.title: Falcon 9 · generic profile
profiles.basis: Generic Falcon 9 profile: typical event order with rounded times, based on SpaceX’s published timelines for recent missions. This mission’s own timeline may differ, especially when and where the payload is released.
events: Nine Merlin engines lift Falcon 9 off the pad.
Peak aerodynamic stress on the rocket.
The nose cone falls away (if the mission uses one).
Most Falcon 9 boosters land on a droneship or landing zone.
When and where the payload is released depends on the mission. Check the mission page on launch day.

profiles.title: Falcon Heavy · generic profile
profiles.basis: Generic Falcon Heavy profile: typical event order with rounded times. Many Falcon Heavy missions go to high orbits, so the real flight can last hours.
events: Twenty-seven engines across three cores light together.
Side boosters cut off and separate
The two side boosters peel away and head back to land.
The two side boosters land back at the Cape.
The second stage reaches a parking orbit.
Depends entirely on the mission; high orbits can take several hours.

profiles.basis: Generic Electron profile: typical event order with rounded times. Rocket Lab publishes each mission’s timeline in its press kit.
events: Nine Rutherford engines lift the small Electron rocket.
The Curie kick stage takes over.
The kick stage releases the satellite.

profiles.title: Starship · generic profile
profiles.basis: Generic Starship profile: typical event order with rounded times from recent test flights. Each flight’s plan differs.
events: Thirty-three Raptor engines lift Super Heavy and Starship.
Most of Super Heavy’s engines shut down.
Starship lights its engines while still attached, then pushes away.
Super Heavy returns to be caught by the tower or splash down.
On some flights Starship releases test or Starlink satellites.
